articles.title: In 2010, a developer paid $1.25 million for two wrecked Brooklyn properties; sixteen years later, the 1852 mansion is listed for $20.99 million following a long rebuild, alongside its renovated carriage house
articles.summary: A Brooklyn Heights mansion once described as a “derelict eyesore” is back on the market after a decade-long reconstruction, alongside its neighbouring
articles.body: A Brooklyn Heights mansion once described as a “derelict eyesore” is back on the market after a decade-long reconstruction, alongside its neighbouring carriage house, with the two properties seeking a combined $20.99 million, the New York Post reported. The adjoining but legally and physically separate properties are being marketed together as Monroe Place Estates, with the 1852 mansion listed for $14.99 million and the renovated carriage house asking $6 million.A 1852 mansion that the city wanted goneThe 1852 Greek Revival home at 1 Monroe Place, in New York City’s first historic district, had been sitting derelict for years. In 2008, the NYC Department of Buildings declared the house structurally unsound. The city removed the building’s top floors and forced its last three rent-stabilised tenants to leave. The owner sued to block a full teardown, but a court threw out the suit in 2010. Months later, the property was sold to a firm run by developer Margaret Streicker, which paid $1.25 million in cash for the wrecked properties.A rebuild that took yearsThough purchasing the property was easy, rebuilding it wasn’t. Landmarks rules, shifting building codes, the pandemic and claims from the displaced tenants all slowed things down. Streicker describes the work as a regulatory puzzle. In her words, the team “unlocked it with a multi-phase, multi-year strategy”, according to the Post’s Gimme Shelter column, which broke the story. They weren’t simply looking to patch up the old building; they rebuilt the house from the ground up.The restoration work was handled by NV Design Architecture. It took almost a decade to rebuild the house. The website says the project began in 2016 and ran until 2026. The team had to re-create the masonry, woodwork and ornamentation using a limited collection of historic photographs and archival records. That was no easy job, and certainly not something that could be rushed. The meticulous work is visible now. The house still looks as though it belongs to the 1850s, but much of what stands there today was built recently.Mallory Bogard, one of the listing agents, told the Post how the neighbourhood had reacted to the restoration. “As we have been preparing it for the market, people have been commenting on what an amazing milestone it is to bring the home back.”What the buyer getsThe Greek Revival home is a five-storey house covering roughly 7,200 square feet. It has a red-brick façade, oversized bay windows, a stoop and a mansard roof. Inside, there are seven bedrooms, seven full bathrooms and four powder rooms.“Far beyond a traditional gut renovation, this remarkable transformation honours the home's historic character while introducing the craftsmanship, infrastructure, and refined comforts of a newly built luxury residence,” the Sotheby’s listing describes it.The home has a chef’s kitchen equipped with Viking, Sub-Zero and Fisher & Paykel appliances, wide-plank hickory floors and an elevator. The full-floor primary suite includes its own gym. A wine cellar, wet bar, playroom and home office round out the main house.Two garden-level studios sit below, each with its own kitchen, bathroom and private entrance. The roof terrace has a gas grill and open views.The carriage house next doorThe carriage house at 94 Clark Street is a three-storey building, also built in 1852 and fully renovated. It spans about 2,100 square feet and has three bedrooms, three and a half bathrooms and a skylit kitchen. Prospective buyers can also purchase the carriage house independently for $6 million. The listing describes the two properties as “a singular residential estate”. They are separate homes that share a wall and can be bought together or separately. Together, the asking price comes to $20.99 million.Serhant’s Mallory and Brandon Bogard hold the listings. According to the listing, this is a rare and extraordinary opportunity to own “a private family compound, a multigenerational sanctuary, a live-work retreat, or a creative startup hub.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Meet Vedant Thakker, the 16-year-old California student who built a free wildfire warning checker showing four location categories and is teaching Fremont seniors how to use it after a nearby brush fire
articles.summary: Vedant Thakker was 16 years old when a brush fire in the hills above his Fremont neighborhood made wildfire risk feel personal.
articles.body: Vedant Thakker was 16 years old when a brush fire in the hills above his Fremont neighborhood made wildfire risk feel personal. The California high school student later built Red Flag Check, a free website and app that lets people enter an address and see whether they are inside a National Weather Service red flag warning zone, downwind of one, adjacent to one, or outside the current warning area. He is now teaching seniors at Fremont’s Age Well Center how to use the tool, according to NBC Bay Area and the Oakland Firesafe Council.The project began with a simple frustration. Red flag warnings often cover large geographic areas, leaving residents unsure whether their own home is actually at risk. Vedant wanted a clearer answer, especially for older adults who may be more vulnerable during fast-moving wildfires.A nearby fire changed his focusLike many teenagers, Vedant had not paid much attention to the news before the brush fire broke out near his Fremont neighborhood. Seeing flames close to home changed that immediately. He recalled thinking that the fire was happening right there, near him, and that it felt unreal. From then on, he began paying closer attention to wildfires and to the red flag warnings issued when weather conditions raise the risk of fire.The problem, he found, was that those warnings did not always tell residents whether their particular address was affected. He wanted to know whether a home was directly at risk, and if so, how much. That question became the foundation for Red Flag Check.What Red Flag Check doesRed Flag Check is available at redflag-check.info and uses live National Weather Service data. Users enter an address and receive one of four location categories: inside the warning zone, in a downwind threat area, adjacent to the warning zone, or outside the current warning area. That distinction matters because wildfire danger is not limited to the exact boundary of a warning. Vedant explained, as per the reports, that people who are not directly inside a warning area may still face a major indirect threat if they are downwind of a fire.The tool is free and is intended for informational use during red flag warning events. The Oakland Firesafe Council notes that it uses publicly available weather and fire data to help residents understand their relative position during dangerous conditions.Built with AI, aimed at seniorsVedant developed the app using publicly available weather and fire data, along with artificial intelligence to help him write the code. NBC Bay Area reported that he may have developed Red Flag Check largely on his own, but he did not create it for himself.For the past few years, Vedant has volunteered at the Fremont Age Well Center, where the seniors he works with have come to feel like family. As he researched wildfires, he learned how vulnerable older adults can be during disasters. He pointed to the 2018 Camp Fire, in which the average age of those who died was 72. That statistic helped make the seniors at the Age Well Center the natural first audience for his app.Teaching seniors to use itVedant is now teaching the seniors how to use Red Flag Check, hoping that more specific information can give them greater confidence when wildfire conditions become dangerous. The app gives them a way to translate a broad regional warning into a more personal assessment of their location.The Oakland Firesafe Council praised the project for recognising a community need and for using volunteer time and programming skills to create a new resource. The organisation also shared the app with residents as part of its wildfire preparedness work.For Vedant, the response from seniors is what makes the effort worthwhile. He said he loves when they appreciate that he thought about them, adding that he feels it is something he should do given the affection they have shown him over the past two years.A tool, not an evacuation alertThe Oakland Firesafe Council is clear that Red Flag Check is not a substitute for official emergency notifications. Residents are encouraged to rely on AC Alert, Genasys Protect and other official channels for evacuation orders and public safety information.The council also warns that people can still be at risk from a wind-driven wildfire even if they are outside a red flag warning area. It advises residents to stay informed, have a plan and be prepared.That framing is important. Vedant’s app does not replace emergency services or evacuation orders. Instead, it gives people a free, address-specific way to understand where they stand during a red flag warning and to take preparedness more seriously.Why the project mattersWildfire warnings often arrive as broad alerts covering cities, counties or entire regions. For someone unfamiliar with maps or weather terminology, it can be difficult to know whether a warning includes their street, their neighborhood or a nearby hillside.Red Flag Check tries to close that gap by turning live government data into four plain-language categories. The tool is especially useful for older adults, who may have less time to react in an emergency and may benefit from clearer, more local information.Vedant’s work shows how a student’s concern for his own neighborhood can become a practical community resource. A brush fire near his Fremont home led him to build a tool that now helps seniors understand wildfire risk, one address at a time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Richard Scott’s son lost High Court challenge over farm promises and 2016 wills; judge also dismissed his stepmother’s claim that his tenancies were shams
articles.summary: A son of businessman Richard Norman Scott lost his High Court challenge over promises he said his father made about the family farm.
articles.body: A son of businessman Richard Norman Scott lost his High Court challenge over promises he said his father made about the family farm. Adam Scott, Richard’s second oldest son, argued that he was entitled to land after spending much of his life working on the farm. He also disputed the validity of two wills made in 2016, which made no provision for him.Richard fathered at least 19 children from various relationships. According to the Judiciary of England and Wales, Mr Justice Richards dismissed all three claims on 29 October 2025. His second wife, Jennifer, was among the defendants, alongside Richard’s estate and five of his children. The case also examined two farm tenancies granted to Adam in the family dispute.Why did Adam Scott challenge his father's promises about the family farmAdam’s proprietary estoppel claim centred on a promise Richard made in 1985 to ‘set Adam up in farming’. The judge found that this referred to opportunities during Richard’s lifetime, rather than ownership of the farm after his death. The promise had been fulfilled by 1994, through tenancies, the right to purchase land and arrangements to farm other land.Richard’s 1995 will set out arrangements involving a 40-year rent and an opportunity for Adam to buy certain farms at probate value. However, his 2003 and 2007 wills showed an intention to withdraw those promises. The judge found Adam knew about the change and did not continue working in reliance on the 1995 promise after learning of his father’s revised intentions.How did Giantswood farm affect Adam's inheritance claimThe judge acknowledged that Adam had suffered disadvantages from working on the farm, including long hours, lost career opportunities, and compromised debt claims against Richard. However, Adam had also received substantial benefits. In 2002, he bought the 100-acre Giantswood farm from his father for £500. After Adam spent about £50,000 dealing with tipped waste, the land was worth around £300,000 in 2004.It also generated agricultural subsidies. Adam was entitled to 50% of the profits from a successful car boot business. After weighing the benefits against the disadvantages, the judge concluded that he had suffered no net detriment after considering all the evidence. Giantswood later gained development potential, and Adam sold 35 acres for £8.75 million in 2021.Court upheld wills that made no provision for AdamAdam challenged Richard’s September and December 2016 wills, arguing that his father lacked testamentary capacity and did not know or approve their contents. Both wills made no provision for Adam. Experts agreed Richard had fronto-temporal dementia and progressive nonfluent aphasia at the time. Although his speech was limited, he could communicate through gestures and sounds.Legal professionals who assessed him in 2016 considered that he had testamentary capacity. The judge found that Richard understood the nature of making a will, the property being disposed of and the claims of those affected. He also concluded that Richard’s decision not to provide for Adam was not caused by his dementia.The judge found Jennifer had not proved the tenancies were shamsJennifer argued that two tenancies Richard granted to Adam in 1988 and 1993 were shams and had no legal effect. She claimed they were devices to allow more car boot sales, help Adam obtain insurance and support a planning application for a house. The judge rejected her arguments. The car boot business did not begin until 1994, so it had not been anticipated when the tenancies were granted.There was insufficient evidence that the tenancies had been relied on to secure insurance or were necessary for that purpose. Planning permission had been granted in 1988, before the 1993 tenancy, and the judge said seeking a better planning case was equally consistent with a genuine tenancy. The judge found that Jennifer had not met the evidential burden and ruled that both tenancies were genuine legal arrangements.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available court records. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the family dispute, the financial arrangements or the property transactions discussed in the case. articles.title: You better not dare be smoking in Broncos head coach Sean Payton's postgame news conference
articles.summary: Sean Payton mistook a reporter's pencil for a cigarette during his postgame presser after the Denver Broncos' Mile High City win over the Panthers.
articles.body: Things are going pretty well for the folks in the Mile High City when it comes to their football team. The Denver Broncos are fresh off a trip to the AFC Championship game less than a year ago, and this year's team is off to a 7-2 start as they lead the pack in a competitive AFC West division. A lot of that is due to the wizardry of head coach Sean Payton, who came onto the scene in Denver in 2023 and turned a franchise that had not been to the playoffs since winning Super Bowl 50 nearly a decade ago into a legitimate contender. Payton's no nonsense approach to coaching coupled with his offensive acumen seems to have been the panacea for a Broncos team in limbo for much of the late 2010s and early 2020s. That no nonsense approach apparently extends to the beat reporters in Denver, too. BRONCOS COACH SEAN PAYTON BURIES GEOFF SCHWARTZ AFTER ANALYST BUTCHERS BO NIX'S DOWNFIELD GAME After the Broncos' 26-21 win over the then-AFC South-leading Carolina Panthers on Sunday afternoon, Payton took the podium to discuss the victory before taking exception to a reporter apparently daring to have a smoke right in the middle of his postgame press conference. There's just one problem: the reporter in question wasn't taking a drag off a Marlboro Red but was just chomping on a good old Dixon Ticonderoga No. 2 pencil. As a man who lost his father-in-law to lung cancer a few years back, I have to commend Coach Payton's stance on smoking, but this was an absolutely wild interaction. You can tell Payton was pretty embarrassed about the whole thing too, but fortunately both he and the reporter took the exchange in stride. MIKE MACDONALD APOLOGIZES TO SEAN PAYTON FOR REVEALING SPYGATE-TYPE ACCUSATIONS BETWEEN BRONCOS AND SEAHAWKS The Super Bowl-winning head coach could barely make it through his answer without busting out in laughter. The good news here is that when Payton decides it's time to hang up the visor and whistle, he has a career as a D.A.R.E. officer at any school district in either the Denver or New Orleans areas. "Hey kids, I'm officer Sean, and I don't care if you're a Super Bowl champion or a Broncos beat writer, I better not EVER catch you smoking or doing drugs! That's not what winners do." articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries supports impeaching Pete Hegseth, and a deadly mass shooting in Poland: Weekend Rundown
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he supports efforts to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which are expected to be brought to a vote this week.
articles.body: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he supports efforts to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which are expected to be brought to a vote this week. Asked in an interview on ABC News’ “This Week” whether he would support Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., in his efforts to impeach Hegseth, Jeffries confirmed he supported the push. “I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. Jeffries’ support is a major endorsement of the effort, and it signals how other House Democrats could ultimately vote. The push also tests how far lawmakers are willing to go to oust the top Defense Department official after voters gave low marks to the administration’s handling of the war in Iran, which was a factor in the midterm elections. Kraków shooting that killed 6 was motivated by far-right views, authorities say Poland has declared two days of national mourning after a shooter motivated by far-right ideology killed six people in Kraków on Saturday in what the country’s defense minister described as a “terror attack.” The gunman, whom officials described as holding “ultranationalistic” beliefs, reportedly opened fire in the city’s Main Market Square, killing four women and two men. A police officer who confronted him was among the 16 people injured and remains in critical condition. Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said the suspect is being investigated on suspicion of murdering six people. He said the attacker “acted with the aim of seriously intimidating a large number of people,” making the shooting a terrorist offense. The man, who was shot by police and remains in critical condition, is also being investigated in the deaths of three relatives found at his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 93 miles northeast of Kraków. Meet the Press Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he hopes Democrats prioritize healthcare and food assistance when they take control of Congress in January. “I hope one of the first things that the Congress does is to stop these Medicaid cuts, stop the SNAP cuts, roll back the cuts, the effective cuts in the Affordable Care Act,” Shapiro said in an interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” “It can’t be either/or,” he said. “It has to be both/and.” Florida Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, in an exclusive interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” said “I actually don’t know what” Gov. Ron DeSantis is talking about after DeSantis blamed midterm losses on GOP “gaslighting.” Asked by moderator Kristen Welker whether Republicans should take responsibility for the state of the economy, he said yes. “If Republicans in my view want to be serious about anything, we have to start having this real political conversation and economic conversation around healthcare to stabilize healthcare costs, lower healthcare costs,” Donalds said. Notable quote Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, who flipped deep-red Kansas for Democrats, told “Meet the Press” that he hopes to prioritize lowering costs for his constituents and that he would be “deeply disappointed” to spend two years investigating members of the Trump administration. Politics in brief Ultimate federal communications: Trump posted on Truth Social that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to UFC head Dana White, who said they had a meeting scheduled Monday. Tee-ing up an investigation: A federal judge said she intends to appoint a former U.S. attorney to examine whether the government misled her in the case over Trump’s renovation of East Potomac Golf Links. Reining in AI: Democrats’ competing priorities and opposition from the Trump administration could complicate efforts to enact new regulations on AI. Israel’s president taps opposition candidate to form a government Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27, a major blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a clear majority in the vote. In marathon discussions with Herzog this week, representatives from most of Israel’s main parties recommended that Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government. The announcement, which had been expected Sunday, came shortly after Netanyahu called for a “national unity government” in a video statement and warned against “hastily swearing in a government with terrorist supporters” — an apparent reference to the Arab-led parties. Nvidia opens investigation after reports CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence The board of Nvidia said Sunday that it was opening an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The announcement followed reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. The two are not related. In a memo to employees shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” James Talarico kicks off ‘SNL’ Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico made a surprise appearance to help kick off the latest episode of “Saturday Night Live.” “SNL’s” cold open featured New York’s Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (played by Kenan Thompson) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (Sarah Sherman) and Trump (James Austin Johnson) before Talarico made his entrance. “Hi, America,” he said. “I’m James Talarico, the guy who’s been texting you every day asking for $5.” Trump responded, “In this economy, who can blame you?” In case you missed it An experimental drug that showed significant promise in lowering a dangerous form of cholesterol has failed to reduce the risk of heart attack or stroke in a major clinical trial. The failure of Novartis’ pelacarsen to benefit people with high levels of lipoprotein(a) stunned researchers.Thousands gathered along the Uruguay River on Saturday for Pope Leo XIV’s first Mass in South America, as he sought to raise the Catholic Church’s profile in Uruguay, one of the region’s most secular countries. A man found outside LeBron James’ Los Angeles home was arrested on suspicion of felony stalking and claimed to be his son, police said.A cyclist was killed and at least 12 others were injured when a driver, suspected of being impaired, plowed into a group of cyclists in North Carolina.Heavy rain has flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians across Gaza, washing away shelters and soaking blankets and mattresses, authorities said.

articles.title: Iran vows ‘astonishing’ strikes and lifts missile-range limit as US targets land routes
articles.summary: Iran's IRGC lifted its 2,000-kilometer ballistic missile-range limit and threatened new weapons hours after U.S. Central Command launched a new task force.
articles.body: Iran lifted its self-imposed ballistic missile-range limit and threatened to unleash new, homegrown weapons that would "astonish the entire world," within hours of the U.S. military launching a new task force aimed at choking off Tehran's weapons shipments and illicit trade Nov. 7. Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi confirmed that Iran was now abandoning its previous 2,000-kilometer, or roughly 1,240-mile, ballistic missile-range restriction, according to The Associated Press. "That restriction has been lifted for us," Mohebbi clarified in the wake of the task force announcement. RUSSIA SECRETLY BOLSTERED IRAN'S MISSILE ARSENAL BEFORE WAR WITH US, RECORDS UNCOVER U.S. Central Command established "Task Force Iron Gate", an initiative targeting the movement of advanced Iranian weapons systems, dual-use materials and illicit revenue across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea. "Strengthening CENTCOM's collaboration with US Interagency partners will further constrain Iran's ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military," Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, said in a statement shared on X. According to Behnam Taleblu, senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), the U.S. may now carry out "targeted strikes" against facilitators while putting "political pressure on bordering states, as well as market and sanctions pressure against institutions underwriting Iran’s illicit trade." "It speaks volumes, of course, that this effort is being stood up within CENTCOM headquarters," Taleblu told Fox News Digital. Meanwhile, Iran's IRGC quickly dismissed the new initiative as "wordplay," claiming Tehran had already made preparations and coordinated with neighboring countries to withstand additional pressure, Fars News Agency reported. Mohebbi also warned that Iran was developing new weapons capable of delivering devastating blows in another confrontation with the U.S. and Israel. IRAN INSTALLS NEW WAR CHIEFS AS TEHRAN SIGNALS ‘PROLONGED CONFRONTATION,’ EXPERT WARNS "There are surprises that will be unveiled and deployed on the battlefield if a third wave of confrontation with the enemy erupts. These surprises will astonish the entire world," Mohebbi said during a news conference in Tehran on Saturday, according to Iran's state-run Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA). "If they once again miscalculate, or if the Zionists, in pursuit of their own interests, lead the criminal United States into another miscalculation, they should know that Iran's next blows will be even harder and will leave them crippled for years to come," he added. Iran's previous 2,000-kilometer limit already placed the entire Arabian Peninsula, the Levant, most of Egypt and parts of Greece and the Balkans within range. In March, Iran unsuccessfully attempted to strike the joint U.S.-British military base on Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean, roughly 2,500 miles from the Islamic Republic. Mohebbi also claimed Iran was preparing to unveil new underground missile facilities, as Tehran seeks to shield its weapons production from future attacks. The installations, described by Iranian officials as "missile cities," are designed to allow the IRGC to continue manufacturing weapons during wartime, according to IRNA. TRUMP'S MOAB THREAT COULD PUT IRAN'S DEEPEST BUNKERS IN AMERICA'S CROSSHAIRS The IRGC spokesman claimed Iran's Aerospace Force continued producing missiles and drones during recent fighting, using domestic expertise without importing foreign weapons or relying on "reverse engineering of weapons captured from the enemy." Mohebbi also described Iran's growing self-sufficiency in weapons production as a "very big achievement." Taleblu meanwhile emphasized the significance of the Caspian Sea basin, saying the world’s largest lake has "turned into a two-way sanctions-busting hub for both Iran and Russia." "Iranian officials always claim self-sufficiency in their military industries," he said. "But with domestic missile production significantly constrained due to the 40-Day War, the regime will be reliant on imports to build back, and especially at scale and at a faster rate. "This is why efforts to constrain both land and sea trade in and out of Iran are a one-two punch for the regime." The warnings come as Washington intensified pressure on Iran's regional trade routes, including its land crossings with Iraq, where Baghdad has reportedly resisted U.S. demands for full and broader border restrictions. According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), Iraq has closed only one border crossing with Iran so far, despite reported American pressure to shut down most crossings between the two countries. FRESH ACTIVITY EMERGES AT IRAN’S DEEPLY BURIED NUCLEAR SITE AS TRUMP WARNS IRAN NOT TO ‘GET CUTE’ On Sunday, the U.S. Treasury pressed Iraq to close all border crossings with Iran except for two as part of Washington's policy of increasing economic pressure on Tehran, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said, according to Reuters. The Iraqi government had closed the al-Shayeb crossing in southeastern Iraq on Oct. 21, to review security and install equipment to prevent smuggling of prohibited materials. Iraqi political sources told Agence France-Presse that Washington had pressured Baghdad to close most Iran-Iraq border crossings to restrict trade and financial exchanges that could help Tehran withstand U.S. sanctions, ISW reported. ISW also said that Iranian Ambassador to Iraq Mohammad Kazem al-Sadegh was pressuring tribal leaders in Iraq's Maysan province to push Iraqi officials and leaders of the Shiite Coordination Framework to reopen al-Shayeb. articles.title: Meet Jacob, the 14-year-old from England who started selling tomato plants from a small cart and now grows 7,000 plants, with customers ordering from overseas
articles.summary: Jacob Mann, 14, from Norwich, England, has turned his love of gardening into a growing business selling tomato plants, growing kits and tomato merchandise.
articles.body: Jacob Mann, 14, from Norwich, England, has turned his love of gardening into a growing business selling tomato plants, growing kits and tomato merchandise. It all started from humble beginnings with a few seedlings and a home-made bicycle trailer, and has grown into The Tomato Cart, growing thousands of plants each year with customers from far and wide, even beyond the UK. Jacob now cultivates up to 7,000 tomato plants to meet demand, with his products attracting buyers as far away as Australia, BBC reports. He started with a family gardening competition during the Covid pandemic.14-year-old Jacob turned a gardening hobby into The Tomato Cart Jacob's interest in growing plants developed during the pandemic, when his family decided to turn their vegetable patch into a friendly competition. While the other plots struggled, his continued to flourish, giving him an early indication that gardening was something he enjoyed and could do well.In a case study published by The Shropshire Seaweed Company, Jacob explained that the experience encouraged him to take growing more seriously. He subsequently began thinking about establishing his own garden centre one day, selling plants he had raised himself.The opportunity to start earning money came a few years later. When his brother began making money through a paper round, Jacob also wanted to earn independently. Rather than simply taking up a conventional job, he decided to build something around his interests.Tomatoes became his starting point because they were enjoyable to grow and could eventually be eaten. He collected a greenhouse found through Freecycle with his father just two days before his 13th birthday in December 2024.He then saved his pocket money to purchase an old trailer base through Gumtree. Together with his father, he turned it into a specially designed cart that could be attached to a bicycle and taken to local markets and car boot sales.The business became The Tomato Cart, allowing Jacob to sell plants directly to customers around Norwich.From a handful of plants to 7,000 in a greenhouseThe early business was modest, but Jacob's growing experience and customer interest helped it expand. BBC reported in March 2026 that he had initially sold approximately 14 plants before demand increased significantly.He had built up a greenhouse containing as many as 7,000 plants. Managing that volume requires considerable work, particularly because tomato plants need regular attention and the growing season is relatively short.He grows thousands of plants each year alongside his school work, the Shropshire Seaweed Company said. He waters plants before school, and his parents help to ensure that his business obligations do not interfere with his education.Weather has also been a considerable challenge. Jacob told the company that unpredictable British conditions, from freezing nights to heatwaves, made growing large numbers of plants difficult. Before installing greenhouse heaters, he sometimes had to bring plants indoors overnight to protect them from the cold.His early days of selling at markets was another obstacle. At first Jacob worried people might not take him seriously because he was so young. He was uncomfortable at first explaining his products to people and appearing in social media videos but through customer support, he slowly got more confident.Why customers keep returning to his tomato cartFor Jacob, selling plants is not simply about making money. One of the most rewarding parts of the business is hearing from customers who have successfully grown tomatoes using his plants.He enjoys seeing photographs of customers' first harvests and hearing how their plants have developed. This feedback makes the time spent sowing seeds, watering plants and preparing them for sale worthwhile.His experience and growing knowledge also allow him to help customers select varieties suited to their gardens. With support and advice from Nick at JustSeed, he has developed a selection ranging from familiar favourites to less common tomato varieties.The business has also received attention beyond local markets. According to the Shropshire Seaweed Company, Jacob has appeared on podcasts, in local newspapers and on radio programmes. He also attended the RHS Sandringham Flower Show, where he met gardening personalities Rekha Mistry, Ade Sellars and Alan Titchmarsh.How The Tomato Cart expanded beyond local marketsAs the number of plants Jacob grows increased, he began looking for ways to reach customers outside Norwich. His business now operates through several channels, including markets, online sales and his own website.The Tomato Cart's official website describes Jacob as a Norwich-area teenager selling tomato plants through a specially designed bicycle trailer. It also advertises home growing kits through Etsy, alongside local delivery and pre-orders.The expansion has helped him address a problem common to seasonal plant businesses. Tomato plants are mainly sold during a limited period of the year, leaving fewer opportunities to generate income during the colder months.Jacob responded by developing products that customers could purchase beyond the main planting season. These include home growing kits, which contain seeds, compost, plant labels, pots and instructions written by him.The website also features a pizza-growing kit containing San Marzano tomato, basil and oregano seeds. The idea allows customers to grow ingredients associated with pizza from their own homes, including on a windowsill before moving the plants outdoors.Another unique addition is Adopt a Tomato, a collection of crocheted tomato keyrings sold with adoption cards. The products give the business a playful identity while allowing Jacob to continue selling something when his greenhouse plants are not ready for customers.BBC reported that his merchandise has attracted international interest, with a customer in Australia purchasing a crocheted tomato mascot. The buyer was around 10,000 miles away, illustrating how a small business operating from Norwich can reach people well beyond its local community.Jacob's ambition is to encourage more people to grow foodHe believes growing tomatoes, herbs or vegetables can help people understand where their food comes from and appreciate the process of producing it. Watching a plant develop from a seed into something edible is central to what he wants customers to experience.His business has also developed a partnership with The Shropshire Seaweed Company, whose organic liquid seaweed fertiliser he already used while growing plants.You use AI every day. articles.title: Chancellor Merz to nominate Aigner as Germany’s first woman president
articles.summary: Ilse Aigner, speaker of the Bavarian state parliament, belongs to the Christian Social Union in Bavaria (CSU) party.
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will nominate Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner for Germany’s next president, which would make her the country’s first female head of state.

Merz made the announcement at a dinner for leaders of his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party on Sunday.

Aigner, speaker of the Bavarian state parliament, belongs to the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the CDU.

If her nomination is confirmed at a CDU and CSU meeting on Monday, she would almost certainly be formally elected.

According to German political practice, coalition parties must agree on a common candidate. The governing coalition is made up of the CDU, the CSU and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

The SPD has frequently voiced its support for Aigner as president.

The German president is elected by the Federal Convention, convened solely to choose the president. It will decide on incumbent Frank-Walter Steinmeier’s successor on January 30.

Steinmeier, a Social Democrat, took office in 2017, and will reach the limit of two five-year terms in March 2027.

Germany’s president holds a largely ceremonial position, signing legislation into law and formally appointing ministers.

But the president can play the role of a neutral arbiter, above party politics, and acts as a symbol of national unity.

The CSU put forward Aigner’s name earlier this year, but the CDU held back from endorsing her while Merz considered alternatives, straining relations between the parties.

Aigner, 61, began her political career in local politics before being elected to federal parliament in 1998.

She served as agriculture minister under former Chancellor Angela Merkel before returning to her home state of Bavaria, where she became speaker of the state parliament in 2018.

articles.title: Trump’s proposed Russia deal raises NATO alarm as ex-commander warns Putin seeks influence over Europe
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says a Russia deal could involve "all of Europe" as retired Gen. Philip Breedlove warns Putin wants spheres of influence.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's push for a deal with Russia to end the war in Ukraine and potentially reshape European security has raised alarm among NATO allies, with a former top alliance commander warning Fox News Digital that President Vladimir Putin has long sought to divide the world into competing spheres of influence. The warning came as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also appeared to reject what he called a potential "Yalta 2.0," and NATO allies debated direct outreach to Putin ahead of delegations preparing for talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11. Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove, the former Supreme Allied Commander Europe, warned that Putin's ambitions extend far beyond Ukraine and reflect a broader vision for how global powers should divide influence. "Putin has a plan for the world, and he has pushed that plan on leaders several times," Breedlove warned before adding: "He talks about it and he writes about it." ZELENSKYY TO SEEK OFFRAMP FOR YEARS-LONG RUSSIA WAR IN UN SPEECH AFTER TRUMP REVEALS PEACE DEAL IS CLOSE Trump had suggested Thursday that an agreement with Moscow could extend beyond ending Russia's nearly five-year war in Ukraine. "It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine... I could even say it might involve all of Europe," Trump told reporters after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House. "It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled," Trump added. Breedlove said Putin has repeatedly promoted a vision of dividing global power among Russia, China and the United States. "The plan is three spheres of influence whereby China controls the Far East, Russia controls Europe, and America controls the Western Hemisphere. I do not expect there's going to be a lot of cooperation from the countries of Europe," he said. "The Western world is waiting to see what this big plan is, and they are very concerned because it is about them," Breedlove added. Zelenskyy also warned Friday against repeating the 1945 Yalta Conference, where Allied leaders negotiated Europe's postwar order before the Soviet Union consolidated control over Eastern Europe. "We don't want to have Yalta 2.0," the Ukrainian leader told CNN. "We don't want to be divided by Russia," he said before adding: "For me, it's not simple and it can be dangerous." On Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that discussions on how Europe would look after the Ukraine war were already underway. "It's one of the key topics that's been raised repeatedly in every conversation, anytime negotiations have been discussed," he said ahead of traveling to Paris for the G7 meeting. RUBIO SOUNDS CAMPAIGN-READY AS HE RAILS AGAINST OPEN BORDERS, GLOBALISM IN SPEECH FROM ANCIENT GREEK RUINS "So I think that's what the president is alluding to, is that there's been some advances made and what that architecture could look like post-conflict. We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point," he added, clarifying Trump's comments. Breedlove, however, questioned whether European governments and Ukraine would even accept a broader agreement negotiated without their involvement. "I do expect that when we get a peek under the hood of what Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump have devised that there may be European partners and allies to include Ukraine that may or may not be enthralled with the proposed solution." "We have always said nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," the expert said. "Neither have we heard anything about the EU or NATO being in this conversation. And yet the EU, NATO and Ukraine are central and the heart of the matter that apparently is going to be discussed." Tensions also appeared to mount further after Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a rare 90-minute telephone conversation with Putin on Oct. 27, according to reports. TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized the separate European diplomatic initiatives. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," she said as Breedlove went on to defend the outreach. "The two calls that recently took place between Northern leaders in the NATO alliance and Russia, I don't think that they're out of place at all," he said. "I think they're entirely appropriate." "The great powers of Europe are getting very concerned that someone is dealing with their security without including them in the conversation," he added. Meanwhile, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot confirmed Sunday that France would participate in the Abu Dhabi negotiations. "The Europeans will be well represented; France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in these discussions," Barrot said, according to Reuters. FORMER UK PRIME MINISTER TONY BLAIR WARNS EUROPE ‘WE DON’T WIN’ IN WAR WITHOUT US SUPPORT Breedlove warned that any agreement requiring European nations to sacrifice their security to satisfy Moscow would still face fierce resistance. "If the maximalist demands of Russia remain intact and in order to find peace, all the rest of Europe has to give up its security, sacrifice its security, make itself more susceptible to Russian attack, then this is not going to go well," he said. "Putin has never been a partner for peace in Ukraine. Putin is not now a partner for peace in Ukraine." "The EU nations, the NATO nations, and Ukraine are not going to sign up to a plan that suggests that Russia will be able to once again amass its armies, march across borders and intervene in its neighbors' internal business." articles.body: RAIPUR: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday warned that the end of armed Maoist insurgency did not mean the threat had disappeared, alleging that what he called 'Dimagi Naxals' had infiltrated political parties and organisations and were inciting people against the Constitution and democracyContinuing his long-standing tradition of celebrating Diwali with security forces, this time at Karanpur camp in Chhattisgarh's Bastar - once the epicentre of Maoist insurgency and declared free of Naxalism on March 31 this year - he called for identifying and defeating such elements to safeguard the country.Calling it a historic Diwali after nearly five decades of conflict, Modi said this was the first festival of lights when every district in the country was free from Maoist insurgency. "This is the first Diwali after the country has won its decades-long battle against Naxalism and Maoist terror. This is the first Diwali when every district is free from Naxalism," he said, attributing the achievement to the courage, sacrifices and dedication of security forces.Modi asserted that for the first time in 47 years, the CRPF had completed a year without losing a single jawan in operational duty.Political will since 2014 drove anti-insurgency success, says PM | page 6He described the milestone as a victory of sound policies, political resolve and the bravery and restraint of security personnel. "More than 1,000 jawans sacrificed their lives in Chhattisgarh", he said, recalling the scale of Maoist violence, adding there was a time when more than 230 districts across 20 states were affected.From Bihar and Odisha to Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, vast regions had lived under the shadow of violence, he said. "After sunset, life would come to a standstill. People could not step out of their homes. Naxals had even snatched away people's right to vote," he said.Modi recalled the April 2010 Dantewada massacre in which 76 CRPF personnel were killed and another attack that year in which he said 44 civilians lost their lives. He accused previous govts of treating the insurgency as an incurable problem and abandoning tribal communities to their fate. "Some had accepted that bullets would continue to fly, jawans would die and innocent people would suffer. No country can confront its enemies with an attitude that things will simply continue this way," he said.He credited the change in India's counter-insurgency strategy to the political will demonstrated after his government assumed office in 2014. "We gave our security forces the freedom to take every necessary decision," he said, adding the govt had taken several national security decisions, including measures not widely known to the public, to disrupt funding networks supporting Maoists and separatist organisations. He also alleged that elements within the earlier political and administrative system had provided support to Left-Wing Extremism, which his govt worked to eliminate.Linking the decline in insurgency to development, Modi said Maoists had prevented schools, hospitals, medical facilities, mobile towers and industries from coming up in areas under their influence. Modi said the govt had, therefore, pursued security operations alongside a special development campaign.According to him, more than 15,000km of roads had been constructed in areas affected by Naxalism, along with over 9,500 mobile towers. Nearly 175 Eklavya residential schools had been opened for tribal students, while 50 industrial training institutes and approximately 50 skill development centres were established to improve employment opportunities. articles.title: Mexican mayor found alive after hours-long abduction
articles.summary: Rio Bravo mayor freed by captors after being abducted in Zacatecas state, known for cartel-linked violence.
articles.body:
The mayor of the Mexican border town of Rio Bravo has been found alive after being abducted in the violence-ridden Zacatecas state in northern Mexico.

Federal officials said Miguel Angel Almaraz was released by his captors on Sunday, hours after being taken to the city of Zacatecas.

He was abducted while travelling with family and friends in a region that straddles the states of Zacatecas and San Luis Potosi on Saturday, when his car was intercepted by armed men, who let the others go.

Almaraz’s relatives were able to reach a town in San Luis Potosi, where they alerted authorities about the incident, according to the state’s Security Department.

Almaraz is the mayor of Rio Bravo, a municipality of about 110,000 people in Tamaulipas state, 11km (7 miles) from Mexico’s border with Texas, United States.

He was acquitted of money laundering charges in 2015, after being imprisoned for six years.

He is a member of the conservative National Action Party, but was previously associated with the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution.

It is unclear why Almaraz was taken. Authorities say they are investigating the case, including who might be involved in the abduction.

Zacatecas state is known for activity involving the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Sinaloa Cartel, both accused of attacking civilians and politicians.

A car bomb exploded outside a municipal police headquarters in Ojo Caliente, Zacatecas state, in August, injuring 11 people and damaging about 30 homes. Officials said the attack may have been retaliation by an organised crime group after a recent arrest.

In June 2021, police discovered the bullet-ridden bodies of 18 men after an apparent gun battle between suspected drug cartels in Zacatecas state.

articles.title: Why now's not the time to put your feet up before Christmas
articles.summary: Small decisions made now can make a big difference to your festive finances, charities say, so here are some tips.
articles.body:
How soon is too soon when it comes to thinking about Christmas and your finances?

The answer, of course, is that it is never too soon. Save early and the cost becomes more manageable.

The squeeze is harder for some than others, with charity Barnardo's warning that some parents will skip meals so their kids get a Christmas dinner with the trimmings.

But, debt advice charity StepChange is offering tips to everyone, to avoid Christmas spending leading to a financially painful new year.

The best way to avoid a difficult January, it says, is to make a realistic plan before the spending begins.

Small decisions now can make a big difference later. Its tips include:

Budget for Christmas in full . So, that's not just presents, a budget should include the cost of food and drink, travel, parties, presents, postage, decorations and other festive extras

. Don't just rely on your December paypacket. Also, make a shopping list before Black Friday on 27 November - it is only a discount if you were going to buy it anyway

Book your train journey now . Advance tickets, if available, are cheaper

Set spending limits . Put a cap on the bill for Christmas socialising, and have a quiet conversation with family and friends about how much to spend on presents

Stocktake before the big food shop . Check your cupboards, fridge and freezer before you go shopping and plan meals around food you already have. Make a list of what you need and compare prices.

Think twice . Can you afford what you are going to buy? Can you afford the repayments if it's bought on credit? And, do you really need it?

"Christmas is a time when we want to enjoy ourselves and make things special for the people we care most about," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive of StepChange.

"But it can also put a lot of pressure on household budgets, and it is key to take steps to get ahead of any January financial blues."

If you are concerned about Christmas leaving you in debt, then it is best to seek advice well before things become unmanageable.

The independent MoneyHelper website has a guide to finding free debt advice near you .

There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, and tips on how to draw up a budget.

And it is really important to watch out for scams at this time of year. Fraudsters will take any opportunity to catch you out, especially when you are under pressure financially.

articles.title: What's your love language - and does it actually mean anything?
articles.summary: The theory of ‘Love Languages’ has no scientific origin but it's often still mentioned in modern dating.
articles.body:
I'm "words of affirmation", and so is my husband. This is supposedly our shared love language.

But, while we do like receiving compliments, they make us both feel a bit awkward.

Despite this, our result was confidently defined when we took the original Love Languages Quiz online, a personality test published by US pastor Gary Chapman who first came up with the five types of expressing and receiving love in 1992.

I'm sceptical. Does the theory really know more about us than our own lived experience of a 10-year marriage?

The five love languages are: Quality Time, Acts of Service, Words of Affirmation, Receiving Gifts, and Physical Touch - and they feel more ubiquitous than ever.

Contestants on dating shows ask each other their love languages; "My love language is…" is a common prompt on dating apps.

According to the Love Languages website, my husband and I are just two out of more than 150 million people to have taken this particular quiz.

Even though we scored much lower on some of the other languages, they speak more directly to us.

For example I love spending "quality time" with my husband, and feel much more loved by him making lists of films to watch with me than when he pays me a compliment.

But where did the idea of these five neat categories come from? And are they relevant for modern dating and relationships?

Unlike other relationship theories - such as attachment theory - the concept of love languages doesn't have scientific origins.

Chapman said the theory came to him after observing couples during counselling sessions he held in his parish.

Counselling psychologist Dr Sarah Emmerson told the BBC that love languages are still mentioned regularly in her sessions.

"There's almost no-one out there who hasn't taken that quiz," she said. "[Couples] quite frequently bring that in and say, 'So my partner is Physical Touch and I'm Acts of Service, so this doesn't work'.

"Research has proven that there isn't a lot of validity to the idea that there are only five ways in which people show love, and that everybody fits neatly into these categories. But people still gravitate towards it, and we have to wonder why that might be."

For some, talking about love languages can simply be a useful introduction to thinking about how they communicate their needs to their partner.

Psychotherapist Georgina Sturmer said that it helps people think about "what you really like in a relationship, and what do other people really like" but points out it's "hugely limited" and risks "oversimplifying everything".

In recent years, many therapists have also warned that Chapman's examples refer too readily to scripture and unequal relationship dynamics.

In the Love Languages book Chapman describes counselling a woman, Ann, whose husband of 10 years is hostile and verbally abusive towards her, including frequently telling her he hates her.

His love language, Ann tells Chapman, is specifically sexual physical touch.

When Ann says she finds it "hard to be sexually responsive" to him, Chapman advises her that she should "rely heavily upon [her] faith in God" to make herself have sex with her husband more often.

This example also exposes another problem - that love languages can be used to coerce partners into showing or receiving love in a way they're not comfortable with.

"There's a risk if someone says, 'well my love language is receiving gifts, so you must give me gifts all the time, or my love language is physical touch, so you must be physically intimate with me all the time," Sturmer said.

The BBC has contacted the Love Languages team for comment.

So what can couples do if they want to understand each other, and themselves, better?

Listen to your partner: "Don't just wait until you can speak, but try to hear what they are saying and acknowledge their feelings," Dr Emmerson said.

"If you reframe your words to lead with your own feelings, it helps you to express what's going on without leaving the other person feeling criticised," Sturmer explained.

Remember that disagreements are normal: "Healthy relationships often feature debate and disagreement," Sturmer said. "The challenge is not about avoiding rupture, it's about finding ways to repair it that can leave the relationship feeling stronger."

But, Dr Emmerson added, you should "pick the right time to talk about things that are difficult - not late at night, not when they've just come through the door".

Respond to bids for connection: Dr Emmerson said you should "try to be emotionally responsive to your partner when they are seeking connection" - even if they're doing so in subtle ways.

"This could be asking for a hug, or just telling you about something they just saw on their phone."

articles.title: Dormouse numbers may be helped by warmer summers - survey
articles.summary: New figures suggest hazel dormice may be recovering after decades of decline, with warmer summers boosting survival.
articles.body:
Dormouse numbers may be recovering in England and Wales after years of decline, offering a rare piece of good news for one of our best-loved mammals.

The animal has disappeared from much of the countryside with conservationists warning of a long-term collapse in its population.

However, new data suggests dormouse numbers increased between 2020-2025, a period that coincided with warmer springs and summers.

Scientists believe these conditions may help dormice survive, by boosting food supplies and reducing the time they spend asleep.

That gives the animals more opportunity to breed and build up fat reserves ahead of winter.

But conservationists caution that many questions remain unanswered, and say protecting the woodlands and hedgerows where dormice live remains essential to their long-term survival.

The only species of dormice in the UK is the hazel dormouse. Once widespread across the country, they are now largely confined to southern England and parts of Wales. They have become much rarer as large areas of woodland are lost and so far native populations have disappeared from around 20 English counties.

The National Dormouse Monitoring Programme, led by the conservation charity People's Trust for Endangered Species (PTES), has been monitoring sites in England and Wales since 1998.

It found that since 2000, dormouse numbers have fallen by almost 60%, equivalent to an average annual decline of 3.5%.

More recently, however, there are signs that trend may be reversing. The data suggests the population increased by almost 10% between 2020 and 2025, although researchers stress there is considerable uncertainty around that estimate.

The apparent improvement coincides with a period of warmer, drier-than-average springs and summers.

Report co-author Ian White of PTES described the "upturn" as "welcome good news" which gives grounds for "cautious optimism".

But he added: "We mustn't lose sight of the bigger picture: populations remain almost 60% lower than they were in 2000."

The hazel dormouse is famous for spending much of the year asleep. It hibernates from around October to May, spending the winter in a nest on the ground.

Even during spring and summer, dormice can go into short periods of deep sleep, known as torpor, when the weather is cold and wet, or food is scarce. This helps the small rodent conserve energy.

Researchers believe warmer summers may be reducing the need for torpor, leaving dormice with more energy for feeding and breeding.

They say more research is needed to understand what longer-term impacts climate change could have on the species.

Dr Charlotte Armitage, an ecologist who worked on the survey, said significant uncertainties remain, including how dormice will respond to warmer, wetter winters.

However, she said warmer summer conditions are likely to give the animals more energy to reproduce and raise additional litters.

"This is good news, but we can't be complacent," she told BBC News.

"We still need to protect their habitat, do more research into the effects of climate change and carry out effective woodland management for the benefit of dormice."

articles.title: Woman says Fayed's brother drugged and sexually abused her at Highland estate
articles.summary: Jill says she was flown to the Fayed family's Balnagown estate, where she was repeatedly assaulted.
articles.body:
A woman has told BBC Scotland how she was trafficked to the Highlands, drugged, sexually assaulted and held prisoner by Salah Fayed, the brother of former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed.

Jill, whose name has been changed for legal reasons, said she was a young Harrods employee when she was recruited to what she believed was an executive training scheme in the 1990s.

Speaking for the first time about the abuse that took place in Scotland, Jill said she was flown on the Fayed family's private jet to Balnagown, their estate in Easter Ross, where she was repeatedly assaulted.

She is one of hundreds of women who have alleged abuse by the Fayed brothers.

Since Mohamed Al Fayed's death in 2023, hundreds of women and girls have alleged they were sexually abused by him.

His brother Salah, who died of pancreatic cancer in 2010, has also been accused of abuse by numerous women.

Police Scotland said three people had been identified in connection with offending against a number of victims at Balnagown and inquiries remained ongoing.

Speaking to BBC Scotland, Jill described Salah Fayed as "a very cruel man" who exploited her vulnerabilities and exercised near-total control over her life.

She said she began her career at Harrods working for Mohamed Al Fayed in a heavily-monitored office staffed largely by young women, where access was tightly controlled and employees were discouraged from interacting with others.

Soon afterwards, she was assigned to work for Salah Fayed.

"I thought it might be better," she said. "Mohamed seemed creepy to me."

Instead, she said, her situation deteriorated rapidly.

"I was taken to Scotland twice. Both times it was on their private jet.

"When you flew there, you flew into Inverness and their vehicles would pick you up from the airport and take you to the estate."

On the Balnagown Estate there were three residences, one for each brother.

Jill describes Salah Fayed's house as smaller than Mohamed Al Fayed's, overlooking the valley with the forest behind and isolated.

She alleged that by this stage Salah Fayed had begun giving her illegal substances.

"The first time he forced me to take the drugs he tried to trick me into taking them," she said.

"He had me locked in a room. He said 'you need to take this, it's good for you'. He lied about what it was and when I refused he screamed at me and forced me to take it.

"The drugs were part of his method of assaulting me."

Jill said he controlled what she ate, wore and who she spoke to.

She said most of what happened was against her will.

"I was isolated, for most of the time," she said. "He was a very cruel man.

"He knew I had some vulnerabilities and he exploited them. He made me feel I was a terrible person."

Jill said escaping the situation was difficult and that she only gradually came to understand the extent of what had happened to her.

"By the time I got away, I was very aware of what he was doing and it took some effort to get away," she said.

"I was by then aware that I could not have been the only one.

"I tried to raise the alarm, I tried to warn people."

Salah Fayed was one of three Fayed brothers who purchased Harrods, the luxury Knightsbridge department store, in 1985.

After his death, Mohamed Al Fayed was accused by more than 20 women of sexual assault in a BBC documentary Predator at Harrods that aired in 2024.

Since those allegations more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line.

Earlier this year, Police Scotland said it was carrying out further investigations into allegations connected to Balnagown Estate.

In a statement, a police spokesperson said: "Three people have been identified in connection with offending against a number of victims.

"Our inquiries are ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further."

The Metropolitan Police is separately investigating allegations linked to Mohamed Al Fayed and those suspected of facilitating his offending.

It said it was one of the largest and most complex investigations it was currently undertaking.

"Seven suspects have so far been interviewed under caution on suspicion of offences including aiding and abetting rape and sexual assault, assisting the commission of sexual offences, and human trafficking for sexual exploitation," a Met Police statement said.

"To date, 168 victims have now come forward. We will continue to assess victim testimonies for evidence of human trafficking."

In a confidential note, shared with survivors, of a meeting between the Met and the All Party Parliamentary Group for Survivors of Fayed and Harrods, it said about 70 people had been referred to the Home Office as potential victims of trafficking.

Al Fayed's brother Salah also abused us, women say

'His hands were everywhere' - women accuse surviving Fayed brother of sexual assault

Police Scotland investigating Al Fayed abuse claims

Jill told BBC Scotland she was aware of other women who alleged they were abused by Salah Fayed in Scotland, although some have never reported their experiences publicly.

She said she agreed with calls from some of the victims for a statutory public inquiry.

And she said she was speaking out because of worries the police investigations were not looking far enough.

Jill has contacted the Metropolitan Police and is also pursuing legal action.

Harrods, which is no longer owned by the Fayed family, said it recognised the "remarkable bravery" of survivors who had come forward and supported them in their pursuit of justice.

The retailer has previously established a redress scheme for survivors of abuse linked to Mohamed Al Fayed.

Jill said any compensation would be a partial refund for the impact on her life.

"You've lost years of your life," she said.

"You've had all these treatment costs, it's impacted your career, impacted your family, so yes they do need to put that right."

"The girl I was when I was sent to that man is gone," Jill said.

"I don't know who she would have been or what her life would have been like.

"My life's work has been recovering from this. It has been a bitter, bitter, decades-long struggle."

The BBC has contacted the Balnagown Estate for comment twice and as yet they have not replied.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Leo Tolstoy: "Even in the valley of the shadow of death, two and two do not make six"
articles.summary: Leo Tolstoy was a Russian novelist and thinker who wrote masterpieces such as \"War and Peace\" and \"Anna Karenina,\" and later in life he turned toward deep
articles.body: Leo Tolstoy was a Russian novelist and thinker who wrote masterpieces such as "War and Peace" and "Anna Karenina," and later in life he turned toward deep questions of morality, faith, and simple living.Tolstoy is widely counted among the greatest writers who ever lived and spoke of ideas that remain timeless and hold relevance even today.Tolstoy’s idea explains that when we put two plain numbers side by side, anyone, from a schoolchild to a retired professor, can see the difference, but sometimes, the situation is such that we do not want to point it out, and we wish the impossible to happen, but that is inevitable, and it is only honesty to actually point out the difference that really matters over everything else.Let’s dig in to know what he exactly means.Quote of the dayEven in the valley of the shadow of death, two and two do not make sixWhat does the quote mean?The quote, which is famously attributed to Leo Tolstoy by Goodreads, might be a translation circulated online over the years with his name, as He was Russian and most of his wording is in the same language.The first half of the line borrows a famous phrase from the Bible's 23rd Psalm. The "valley of the shadow of death" stands for the worst moments of life: fear, grief, danger, loss. The second half is plain arithmetic. Tolstoy put them together, and they say that even in our darkest hour, facts stay facts.When we are frightened or desperate, the mind wants to change reality. A patient wants the report to say something different. A person in debt wants the numbers to work out. A crowd under pressure wants to believe whatever makes the fear go away. Leo Tolstoy tells us that wishing doesn't change the sum, and truth doesn't change because we are suffering, and it doesn't grow because we are afraid.He also applauds the courage behind this. Saying "two and two make four" is easy in a classroom and hard when everyone around you insists on six. The line suggests that honesty matters most when it costs the most.How are these words relevant even today?Think of how we live now. Social media rewards the most viral media, not the most accurate ones. Rumours spread during crises, and people pick up whatever they want to hear fastest. Even today, Tolstoy’s words are a small anchor against all this. It tells us to pause, check, and refuse to trade facts for comfort.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Tensions flare as demonstrators target Jewish restaurants, drawing massive counterprotest
articles.summary: The demonstration targeted six restaurants in Philadelphia’s Rittenhouse Square as Jewish and pro-Israel groups organized a counterprotest.
articles.body: Tensions flared in a Philadelphia neighborhood Sunday after a bike ride organized to boycott several Jewish-owned restaurants sparked overwhelming backlash from the city's Jewish and pro-Israel communities. The "boycott ride" targeted at least six restaurants in Philadelphia's Rittenhouse Square, labeling them "Zionist establishments" and calling for them to leave, according to pro-Palestinian group Philly Bike On Your Left, which organized the event. As riders cycled through the streets waving Palestinian flags, hundreds of Jewish and pro-Israel community members turned out to oppose the demonstration, with heated exchanges unfolding across several city blocks. Dozens of diners also lined up outside the targeted restaurants in a show of solidarity with the Jewish-owned businesses. The boycott also drew sharp criticism for taking place on the eve of the anniversary of Kristallnacht, the 1938 Nazi pogrom against Jews in Germany and Austria marked by widespread anti-Jewish violence, including attacks on homes, synagogues and businesses. PHILADELPHIA 'BOYCOTT RIDE' TARGETING JEWISH BUSINESSES DRAWS CONDEMNATION FROM CITY, STATE LEADERSHIP The Philadelphia police told Fox News that at least three people were arrested in connection with the protest, including a woman accused of assault, a man accused of disorderly conduct and a 17-year-old male accused of assaulting police. Meanwhile, a female counterprotester reported being assaulted by an unknown individual. Two officers also sustained minor injuries during the arrest of one individual, according to the outlet. Neither required medical treatment. No property damage was reported, and conditions returned to normal by late afternoon, police said. Police said about 500 people participated in total, including roughly 300 pro-Palestinian demonstrators, 200 of whom were on bicycles, and 200 pro-Israeli counterprotesters. ANTI-ISRAEL AGITATORS CLASH WITH NYPD OFFICERS NEAR SYNAGOGUE Videos circulating on social media showed demonstrators and counterprotesters shouting at one another. In one video, a restaurant displayed a Palestinian flag alongside a sign reading "No public restroom" on its entrance door. A man confronted the restaurant on camera, accusing it of sending a message that the Jewish community was not welcome. The protest, organized in late October, targeted six businesses whose owners organizers accused of being "Zionist business owners." "We see them for the disgusting humans they are," the group said. "There are business owners in our community who have raised funds for the Israeli military, hosted Israeli soldiers, were praised by Benjamin Netanyahu, or expressed support for Israel," the group added. The demonstration prompted the Jewish Federation of Greater Philadelphia to call for a counter-demonstration in early November. GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS "This is antisemitism. It is Jew-Hatred, plain and simple," the organization said. "The ride falls on the eve of the anniversary of Kristallnacht, November 9-10, 1938, when Nazi-organized mobs destroyed thousands of Jewish businesses, homes and synagogues in Germany and Austria, while thousands of Jews were beaten, assaulted and sent to concentration camps. The public targeting of Jewish businesses should alarm every person of conscience. We cannot allow such hatred to become normalized in Philadelphia." articles.title: Drone attack suspends production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gasfield
articles.summary: The strike leaves more than 70 percent of northern Iraq’s Kurdish region without power.
articles.body:
A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has caused a fire at the facility and cut power to the region, according to Iraqi and Kurdish officials.

The Sunday night attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power.

It was not clear who was responsible for the attack or whether it was related to the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.

Al Jazeera’s fact-checking agency Sanad has verified footage of smoke and flames rising from the vicinity of the gasfield in the Sulaimaniyah governorate.

Omid Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Electricity, said the attack suspended gas supply to power plants in the cities of Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.

The strike knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts of electricity generation off the grid, he said.

He added that the ministry would provide electricity to critical facilities, such as hospitals and water treatment plants, by operating hydroelectric power stations and other plants that run on alternative fuel.

Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, cited security sources as saying the explosive-laden drone struck the Khor Mor gas storage facility, reducing the energy grid’s capacity by 70 to 80 percent.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said there were no casualties as a result of the attack, based on an initial assessment, the INA reported.

Al-Zaidi also directed that a joint investigative committee be formed with the relevant authorities in the Kurdish region to investigate the circumstances surrounding the attack, INA reported.

The attack comes amid heightened regional tensions. A drone strike hit the same facility last year, with no group having claimed responsibility.

articles.title: Dallas public defender’s chief investigator charged with wife’s murder after bloody apartment discovery
articles.summary: Jimmy Spurger Jr., a Dallas County capital murder investigator, is accused of stabbing his wife Maria just days after filing divorce papers.
articles.body: A Texas investigator who spent years working on capital murder cases is now accused of killing his wife of roughly 35 years, less than two weeks after filing for divorce. Jimmy Spurger Jr., 54, the chief investigator for the Dallas County Public Defender’s Office, faces a first-degree felony murder charge after his wife, Maria Spurger, was found stabbed to death inside their downtown Dallas apartment Friday night. Emergency crews found Maria on a couch with a knife in her neck and her husband sitting on a bed in another room, covered in blood, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by Fox 4 Dallas. Spurger filed for divorce Oct. 26, less than two weeks before the killing, according to Dallas County court records. The case was still open, with a Nov. 3 entry indicating Maria had not been served with the divorce papers.TEACHER FOUND DEAD WITH THROAT SLIT; DETECTIVES SCRUTINIZE HUSBAND’S SHIFTING STORY Dallas County Judge Clay Lewis Jenkins said Sunday that he had ordered Spurger suspended and his access revoked. "Upon notice of this tragic murder yesterday, I instructed Administration to place the employee on suspension and remove his access," Jenkins wrote on X. Firefighters received a welfare check call around 10:40 p.m. Friday and went to the couple’s apartment on North Akard Street, according to the affidavit. No one answered their repeated knocks. When firefighters forced the door open, they found furniture blocking the entrance. They moved it aside and found Maria unresponsive on the couch. Spurger was sitting on a bed in the bedroom, but he did not answer when firefighters asked whether he was OK. The crews backed out and called police. Officers arrived around 11:13 p.m. and found Spurger covered in blood, with a small knife beside him. Several empty pill bottles covered in blood were in the kitchen, according to the affidavit. No one else was found inside. IVY LEAGUE-EDUCATED PEDIATRICIAN ALLEGEDLY MURDERED BY HUSBAND WHO THEN SET HOME ON FIRE: POLICE Maria was pronounced dead at the apartment. Spurger was taken to Methodist Central Hospital, and investigators said they could not interview him because he may have taken multiple pills. He was booked into the Dallas County Jail Saturday on a murder charge and is being held without bond, according to jail records. RETIRED POLICE SERGEANT SHOOTS DEPUTY CHIEF WIFE AND THEIR DAUGHTER IN WEALTHY, COASTAL ENCLAVE HOME Before his arrest, Spurger oversaw investigators who helped public defenders prepare criminal cases, according to the Dallas County Public Defender’s Office website. His biography says he served as chief investigator for 11 months. He spent more than 13 years with the office, primarily in its Capital Murder Division, where his work included examining evidence and interviewing witnesses. FORMER CORRECTIONS OFFICER ACCUSED OF KILLING WIFE, FORCING KIDS TO HELP Before joining the public defender’s office, Spurger spent more than 20 years in law enforcement, specializing in homicide investigations and crimes against people, according to the website. During his final decade in law enforcement, he supervised child abuse and family violence investigations for the Dallas County District Attorney’s Office. Police have not released a motive and said the killing remains under investigation. Anyone with information is asked to contact Detective C. Johnson at 214-671-3584 or chanesia.johnson@dallaspolice.gov.
